summary.text:
A district-scale investment monitor written for a council that does not, in this paper, discuss borrowing. Position at 31 December 2025: £41.5M invested at a 4.25% weighted rate, 82% of it lent to 16 other local authorities (para 8.5). The 26-line table publishes each counterparty, principal, coupon, tenor and historic risk of default — that level of line-by-line disclosure is not universal in quarterly monitoring reports and is what the email leans on.

Nine-month interest of £1.869M against a £51.6M average balance (paras 8.2, 8.3) implies an effective annualised yield of 4.83% across the period, higher than the 4.2% year-end book yield because earlier quarters carried higher rates and some of the total is accrued interest from 2024/25 deals. The full-year forecast is £2.000M, up £0.020M on Q2 (para 1.2). Composition ties exactly to the para 8.4 split (Banks 11%, BS 0%, Government 7%, LAs 82%).

No loan-book reconciliation is available: the paper prints no debt table because the council does not carry material long-term debt. Our own file holds 21 legacy micro-loans totalling £305k at 10.96% weighted, but --as-at 2025-12-31 returns 'no loans outstanding' on start-date grounds, so it is a coverage gap either way. The balance-sheet identity cannot be tested — no CFR, no external debt, no OLTL is printed. What the paper does give us is a rare view of the lender side of the inter-authority market, with two rows (Bradford £1.0M at 4.25%, Medway £2.0M at 4.35%) cross-checkable against papers we already hold from the borrower side. Advisor: MUFG (para 5.1).

officer.subject: Your investment table names sixteen councils — we've read one of them from the other side
officer.body:
Dear Ian,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Third Quarter Treasury Management Review that went to your Finance, Audit and Risk Committee on 25 March. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is clearly laid out and the 26-line table at paragraph 8.5 is more disclosure than a lot of quarterly monitors give — this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A scope note first, because it matters. What we hold is the Q3 paper at 31 December 2025, so everything below sits on that date. If the 2025/26 outturn has moved things on since, that is our position being stale rather than yours.

The reading that stood out is the shape of paragraph 8.5. Eighty-two per cent of £41.5m, so about £34m, is out on short-term deposit with sixteen other local authorities at a weighted 4.20% across those rows. Six of those rows sit inside a fortnight of year-end, and the tenors extend out to a £2m line with Walsall at 4.25% for 265 days. That level of line-by-line disclosure — counterparty, principal, coupon, tenor and historic risk of default on every row — is not universal in quarterly treasury monitors, and it makes the paper more useful to read than most.

Here is why that is interesting to us and possibly to you. We read every council's treasury papers, and we have spent this summer reading the other side of some of those trades. Your row for City of Bradford — £1.0m at 4.25% for 56 days — is one we can cross-check because we hold Bradford's own treasury paper, and Bradford is running around £161m of borrowing from other councils across its book. Your row is one of the smaller pieces of that £161m, and the rate you took is consistent with the range Bradford is paying elsewhere. Nobody publishes this market as a whole — every council sees its own trades and none sees the distribution — so a single row that ties to a counterparty's own aggregate is a useful check on the shape of what's out there.

One other observation on the same table. The two DMO lines sit at 3.77% and 3.79% for a fortnight of money, and the LA rows in the same maturity band sit between 4.05% and 4.35%. That 30-45bp spread over DMO for short tenors is roughly where the market still is in mid-August — Bank Rate is unchanged at 3.75%, the further cut some strategies leaned on early in 2026/27 has not happened, and short LA money is still trading at that kind of premium over risk-free.

Where you might find us most useful, given that the paper is investment-only: our monthly PWLB sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows every loan the sector drew that month by council and tenor — which for a lender is the calendar of when councils come to the market. Thin PWLB months are precisely when councils look to the inter-authority market instead, and the rate a lender can ask goes up. July's PWLB was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%; the pattern is on the page.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway becomes central to how treasury strategy is framed even for councils whose current position is fully cash-funded. An interactive version tied to our rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, and a council that is a net investor today has as much interest in seeing how the sector's aggregate borrowing shape moves as a heavy borrower does.

On training, three fit North Herts. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes directly to paragraph 8.5. LA Credit Analysis covers the counterparty side of the same trades and the historic-risk-of-default framework the paper uses. Investment strategy & credit risk sits alongside both. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
